name: Balistarii with Ballista

abilities.name: Barrage
abilities.text: Loose projectiles more frequently for an extended period of time.

attributes.name: Cannot Run
attributes.text: This unit cannot run and will only move at walking pace.

short: A two-shouldered torsion machine, it has a higher firing range than the onager, but most importantly, it is more accurate. The most powerful throwing machines in the Late Roman period were the ballista and the onager (Veg., IV, 29). Ballistarii (Latin) - soldiers assigned as personnel to throwing machines, including ballistae. In case of their unavailability, the manuballista (hand ballista) became their primary weapon. Their equipment probably consisted of a short spear and a small shield - illustrated in the Notitia Dignitatum. An experienced ballistarius could hit a target beyond the reach of arrows fired from a bow. Thus, during the siege of Amida, when the Chionitae king Grumbates and his retinue approached the walls to negotiate, his son was immediately killed by a shot from a ballista (Amm., XIX, 1,7). According to Zosimus, an arrow fired from a ballista could pierce two, three or more people at once (Zos., III, 21,2). In addition to stone bombs, pots with ignition mixture could be used as projectiles in the 4th century.
history: One of the simplest forms of one-armed catapult, the onager relied on twisted skeins of animal sinew which provided the power to hurl either rocks or shot. Inaccurate but powerful, it was an effective siege machine against buildings and fortifications, but was of far less use on the battlefield unless firing into massed infantry ranks. First mentioned by Philon of Byzantium in his treatise on ‘Mechanics’, the onager made use of a sling-like cradle attached to a firing arm. This arm was inserted, twisted, and propelled rocks or shot through torsion. As the firing arm was released, the sling-like cradle would unhook, firing the projectile. A padded beam was incorporated into the housing frame to restrain the arm. Larger machines could require as many as eight or ten crewmen, and the incredible recoil meant that they could not be easily or safely mounted on walls or towers. Quickly constructed wherever wood was readily available, onagers soon became a staple of ancient siege warfare.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
